::: {.callout-important}
Superseded by [TensorRT-LLM: rejected as a runtime, not rejected as a kernel
source](../2026-09-05-tensorrt-llm-kernels/). Objections 1, 3 and 4 below do not
hold: the model zoo gap is work rather than a barrier, `sm_121` is a build flag,
and the kernels are open. The findings below are left unedited as history.
:::

## Question

Should wildfire be built on TensorRT-LLM rather than on its own compiler and
kernels? TRT-LLM is superficially aligned with the doctrine in SPEC section 3:
it is an ahead-of-time graph compiler with a thin runtime, which is exactly the
shape wildfire is aiming for.

## Setup

| | |
| --- | --- |
| node | head |
| kernel | 6.17.0-1031-nvidia-64k, 64 KiB pages, arm64 |
| target | GB10, compute capability 12.1 (`sm_121`) |

No installation was performed. This entry is packaging and architecture
analysis; the commands are in `evidence/packaging-check.txt`.

## Result

**The packaging objection is dead.** An earlier local note concluded TRT-LLM was
unavailable on aarch64 after a PyPI install attempt. That is true of PyPI and
only PyPI: `tensorrt-llm` there is 1.2.1 with an sdist and **zero wheels across
every release**. NVIDIA publishes wheels from its own index instead, where there
are 93 distinct aarch64 wheels, current at `1.3.0rc9-cp312-cp312-linux_aarch64`.
Anyone repeating that install attempt should point pip at the NVIDIA index.

What actually decides it is fit, in this order.

1. **The model is not in the zoo.** GLM-5.3-Flash combines KDA linear attention,
   NoPE sparse MLA with a top-2048 DSA indexer, a 288-expert top-8 MoE, and an
   MTP draft head. None of that is a stock TRT-LLM model definition. Adopting
   TRT-LLM means writing plugins for every interesting layer — so we write the
   kernels regardless, and additionally inherit the graph and runtime
   constraints of a system we did not design.
2. **Our differentiator lives inside its abstractions.** The two things wildfire
   is actually for are the atomic `(KV pages, KDA state)` cache entry from SPEC
   section 6 and compile-time expert placement from section 5. Those live in the
   KV cache manager and the graph builder — precisely the components TRT-LLM
   owns. Building there puts us back to patching a framework, which is the
   posture the spec exists to leave.
3. **`sm_121` coverage is unproven.** NVIDIA's published support matrix names
   Blackwell SM100, SM103 and SM120. GB10 is `sm_121`. The one prior occasion
   TRT-LLM kernels ran on this hardware, the `TllmGenFmhaRunner` refused with
   "Unsupported architecture". That is not proof they cannot work, but it means
   tuned kernels for our SM cannot be assumed.
4. **Closed kernels contradict the thesis.** Getting closer to the hardware
   means being able to fix a kernel for our SM. With CUTLASS or CuTe we can.
   With shipped TRT-LLM kernels we file a bug and wait.

## Verdict

Rejected as wildfire's runtime. The compiler and kernels stay ours; CUTLASS
(4.6.2 is already available in the working image and targets sm_120/121) is the
source for the 4-bit grouped expert GEMM, and TRT-LLM's open kernel sources
remain worth reading as reference.

This is a fit-and-cost decision, **not** a measured performance loss. TRT-LLM
may well be faster on the layers it supports. Reopen this if either holds:

- NVIDIA ships `sm_121`-tuned kernels together with a model definition covering
  hybrid linear attention and sparse MLA, removing objections 1 and 3 at once.
- Our own grouped expert GEMM lands far enough below achievable bandwidth that
  an isolated microbenchmark shows TRT-LLM's grouped GEMM beating it on `sm_121`.
